vignette:
The Weight of Altitude

Marcus is a 53-year-old Māori man who has spent the better part of three decades guiding aircraft through the skies above the Pacific. He is the kind of man who chose aviation because it made sense to him - systems, checklists, the clean logic of instruments. He married young, raised two sons, and built a life that felt, for a long time, like something earned through discipline and care.

Twelve years ago, Marcus was taken.

He had been on a layover in a politically unstable region when he was detained by a paramilitary group, mistaken - or so he was told later - for someone else entirely. For nine days, he was held in a concrete room with no windows. He was beaten methodically. He was deprived of sleep through noise and cold and intermittent electric shock. Men spoke to him in a language he did not fully understand, and the gaps in comprehension made everything worse, because his mind filled them with certainty of death. He survived because a local contact raised an alarm and diplomatic pressure was quietly applied. He was released without explanation, driven to a roadside, and left there in the early morning dark.

He told almost no one what had happened. He returned to flying within six weeks because he believed, genuinely, that returning to the cockpit would restore him. For a time, it seemed to work. The preflight checks, the radio protocols, the shared language of the flight deck - these things held him together like a splint holds a broken limb.

But the fracture never healed.

Marcus now sits across from his therapist with his hands folded in his lap, and there is something careful about the way he holds himself - as though stillness is a form of control he cannot afford to surrender. He sleeps poorly, waking between two and four in the morning with his heart hammering and his sheets soaked through. The dreams are not always explicit. Sometimes they are only darkness and the sensation of cold, and he wakes not knowing where he is, reaching for his wife Aroha, who has learned to speak softly when she touches him in the night.

At work, he functions. His co-pilots describe him as precise and calm. What they do not see is that he has begun to dread certain flight conditions - particularly long overnight routes where the cockpit goes quiet and the darkness outside the windscreen becomes absolute. In those hours, something loosens in him. He finds himself scanning the instrument panel not for information but for reassurance that he exists, that the world outside is real. He has never made an error, and this fact has become something he clings to with a ferocity that exhausts him.

On the ground, he avoids crowded spaces. He does not go to restaurants where he cannot sit with his back to a wall. He has stopped attending the community events he once loved - the kapa haka performances his sons participate in, the gatherings where his extended whānau come together. He tells Aroha he is tired, and this is true, but it is not the whole truth. The whole truth is that he no longer fully trusts the safety of any room.

He describes a persistent sense of being observed, of waiting for something to happen. He does not use the word fear. He says he is alert. He says he is prepared. His therapist notices that he corrects himself whenever an emotion surfaces, substituting a more operational word, as though feeling something is a kind of instrument failure.

What Marcus finds most difficult to say aloud is this: he no longer recognizes the man he was before that concrete room. He looks at photographs from his sons' childhoods and sees someone who moved through the world without bracing for it. He misses that man. He is not sure that man is coming back, and on the long overnight flights, somewhere over a dark and featureless ocean, that uncertainty is the heaviest thing he carries.
